hero.title: The 5 love languages: find yours in 30 questions
hero.description: 30 questions to identify how you express and receive love. A test based on Gary Chapman's 5 Love Languages theory.

intro.p1: We all have a preferred way of expressing love and feeling loved. What Gary Chapman calls the 5 Love Languages has become one of the most widely used tools in couples therapy worldwide. This test lets you discover yours in just a few minutes, completely free, no sign-up required.
intro.p2: Understanding your love language means seeing your relationship in a whole new light. It explains why certain gestures touch you deeply while others leave you cold, and why your partner doesn't always react the way you hope. This love language test is the first step toward smoother, more authentic communication within your relationship.

section1.title: What are the 5 Love Languages?
section1.p1: The 5 Love Languages theory was developed by Gary Chapman, an American marriage counselor, in his book published in 1992. After years of working with couples in crisis, he noticed a recurring pattern: partners genuinely loved each other, but couldn't express it in a way the other person could truly receive.
section1.p2: Chapman identified five fundamental ways that people express and perceive love: Words of Affirmation, Acts of Service, Receiving Gifts, Quality Time, and Physical Touch. Each person has a dominant language that determines what makes them feel truly loved.
section1.p3: This concept has transformed the way millions of couples communicate around the world. By understanding that your partner doesn't perceive love the same way you do, you stop blaming them for a lack of affection and start learning to speak their language. It's a simple but profoundly transformative shift in perspective, similar to what many couples experience when they test their compatibility for the first time.

section2.title: The 5 Love Languages explained in detail
section2.intro: Each love language corresponds to a deep emotional need. Knowing them helps you not only understand yourself better, but also love your partner more effectively. Here's a detailed look at each of the five languages identified by Gary Chapman.
section2.lang1Text: For people whose primary language is Words of Affirmation, words hold immense power. A sincere compliment, well-timed encouragement, or a simple "I'm proud of you" can light up their entire day. On the flip side, criticism and hurtful words leave deep and lasting marks. These people need to hear explicitly that they are loved, appreciated, and valued.
section2.lang1Examples: Real-life examples: sincere compliments about appearance or qualities, words of encouragement during tough times, saying "I love you" daily, sweet messages sent during the day, expressing thanks for small gestures.
section2.lang2Text: For those who speak the language of Acts of Service, love is shown through actions. It's not what you say that counts, it's what you do. Making dinner, unloading the car, scheduling a doctor's appointment for the other person: these concrete gestures are seen as true declarations of love. The core idea is simple: lightening your partner's load is a tangible proof of care and devotion.
section2.lang2Examples: Real-life examples: making a meal without being asked, doing the grocery shopping, fixing something around the house, organizing an outing from start to finish, taking on a chore your partner can't stand.
section2.lang3Text: The Gifts love language isn't about materialism. It's about the symbolism behind the gesture: someone thought of you, took the time to choose something that truly fits you. For these people, a gift is physical proof that they're on their partner's mind. The absence of gifts or forgetting important dates can feel like a deep lack of interest.
section2.lang3Examples: Real-life examples: a small gift picked up during errands, flowers for no particular reason, an object that recalls a shared memory, a personalized gift for an anniversary, a handwritten letter.
section2.lang4Text: People who value Quality Time need full and complete presence. It's not enough to be in the same room, what matters is undivided attention, eye contact, and active listening. A phone-free dinner for two, a hand-in-hand walk, a deep evening conversation means far more than an expensive piece of jewelry. For these people, the time you give them is the measure of your love.
section2.lang4Examples: Real-life examples: a screen-free dinner, a distraction-free walk for two, a board game night, a shared activity (cooking, sports, gardening), a vacation planned together.
section2.lang5Text: Physical Touch goes well beyond sexuality. It encompasses every form of physical contact that creates a sense of safety and connection: holding hands, a caress through the hair, a spontaneous hug, a hand resting on the shoulder. For people whose dominant language this is, physical contact is the primary channel through which they receive love. The absence of touch can create a deep sense of isolation, even within a relationship.
section2.lang5Examples: Real-life examples: holding hands while walking, morning and bedtime cuddles, hair caresses during a movie, massages, physical closeness on the couch.

section3.title: Why knowing your love language changes everything in a relationship
section3.p1: The main source of frustration in a relationship isn't a lack of love, it's the mismatch in how it's expressed. You can love your partner deeply and still make them feel unloved, simply because you don't speak the same language. This silent misunderstanding is behind many tensions that get wrongly blamed on a lack of feelings.
section3.p2: Imagine your language is Physical Touch and your partner's is Words of Affirmation. You shower them with hugs and tender gestures, but what they really need are sweet words and compliments. Each of you gives what you'd love to receive, without realizing the other person needs something entirely different. When this gap goes unidentified, it can lead to a growing sense of being misunderstood.
section3.p3: Knowing your own language and your partner's lets you break free from this cycle. It's like finally getting the owner's manual for your relationship. You understand why certain gestures move your partner and why others fall flat. This awareness, combined with an honest look at your common points as a couple, can transform the dynamic of your relationship in lasting ways.
section3.quote: Loving isn't enough. You also need to love in the language the other person can hear.

section4.title: How to interpret your test results
section4.p1: At the end of the test, you'll get a detailed profile showing your scores for each of the five languages. Your result isn't a fixed diagnosis, it's a snapshot of your current emotional preferences, a starting point for better self-understanding and more effective communication with your partner.
section4.p2: Most people have a clearly identifiable dominant language, along with a secondary language that also plays an important role. It's rare to score 100% in one language and zero in all others. Your profile is more like a spectrum, with stronger or weaker preferences for each language.
section4.tip1Text: This is the language with the highest score. It represents the way you most need to receive love in order to feel fulfilled in your relationship. Share it clearly with your partner, it's not a demand, it's a key to loving you better.
section4.tip2Text: Don't overlook your second language. It complements your dominant one and often kicks in during specific situations. For example, your primary language might be Quality Time, but Words of Affirmation take over during periods of stress or self-doubt.
section4.tip3Title: What if both partners take the test?
section4.tip3Text: That's where the magic happens. When each partner knows their own language and the other's, you have a genuine roadmap for your relationship. You know exactly which gestures have the greatest impact and how to express your love in a way your partner can truly receive. A great follow-up is to play who knows their partner best to see how well you already understand each other.

section5.title: What to do when you and your partner speak different love languages
section5.intro: In the vast majority of couples, partners don't share the same love language. This is not only normal, it's actually an opportunity to enrich your relationship. The difference isn't an obstacle, it's an invitation to grow together.
section5.step1Text: Your partner's language is neither better nor worse than yours. Someone who needs Physical Touch isn't "too clingy," and someone who values Acts of Service isn't "too demanding." Every language is valid and deserves respect. The first step is to welcome this difference with kindness rather than frustration.
section5.step2Text: Just like a foreign language, it takes practice. If your partner's language is Words of Affirmation and it doesn't come naturally to you, start small: one compliment a day, a gratitude message, a sincere "thank you." It may feel forced at first, but over time it becomes second nature. What matters most is the sincerity of your intention.
section5.step3Text: Your partner can't guess your love language. Rather than complaining about what's missing, express what you need in a positive way: "I'd love for us to have an evening just for the two of us" or "It means so much when you tell me you're proud of me." Guiding with gentleness is far more effective than criticizing with resentment.
section5.step4Title: 4. Create rituals that honor both languages
section5.step4Text: Build habits together that nourish both love languages. If one of you needs Quality Time and the other needs Physical Touch, a movie night snuggled up together satisfies both. Look for these points of overlap and turn them into regular rituals. Couples who also dare to answer spicy questions together often strengthen their intimacy in surprising ways.

section6.title: Bringing the love languages into your daily life
section6.p1: Knowing your love language only matters if you put it into practice. The good news is that it doesn't require a big budget or special planning. It's about small, intentional gestures repeated day after day, which end up transforming the quality of your relationship in profound ways.
section6.p2: The most common mistake is waiting for big occasions to express your love. But it's in everyday gestures that love languages truly come alive. It's not the Valentine's Day bouquet that makes the difference, it's the consistency of small, thoughtful acts throughout the year.
section6.idea1Text: Start the day with a gesture tailored to your partner's language: a hug for Physical Touch, a "Have a great day, I believe in you" for Words of Affirmation, a ready-made coffee for Acts of Service, a little note slipped into their bag for Gifts, or five minutes of focused conversation for Quality Time.
section6.idea2Text: A message sent during your lunch break, a quick call to check in, a photo of something that made you think of them. These micro-connections keep the bond alive even when distance and obligations pull you apart. Every love language can be expressed through a simple smartphone.
section6.idea3Text: Coming home is a key moment. Put your phone down, truly listen to your partner's recap of their day, share a moment of physical closeness, or surprise them with an unexpected little treat. The last few minutes before bedtime are especially precious for nurturing your emotional connection.
section6.idea4Text: It's during conflicts and stressful periods that love languages become most valuable. Rather than withdrawing into yourself, use your partner's language to defuse the tension. A tender gesture, a reassuring word, or a heartfelt act of service can turn a moment of crisis into a moment of closeness. When communication breaks down entirely, having a structured way to work through a relationship problem helps move past the deadlock.

section7.title: Is this test reliable?
section7.p1: This test is based on Gary Chapman's 5 Love Languages theory, which has been translated into over 50 languages and read by tens of millions of people worldwide. This approach is used daily by couples therapists and marriage counselors as a tool for mediation and mutual understanding.
section7.p2: It's important to keep in mind that this test is a tool for reflection and dialogue, not a clinical diagnosis. It doesn't replace couples therapy or professional support. Your results may shift depending on the phase of your life, your stress level, or the maturity of your relationship.
section7.p3: The goal isn't to put a permanent label on how you love, but to open a conversation with your partner. Take the test separately, compare your results, and use them as a starting point to build a more attentive and fulfilling relationship.

section8.title: The questions people ask once they've taken the test
section8.sub1Title: How to work out your partner's love language without making them take the test
section8.sub1Text: Listen to what they ask for. People almost always ask for whatever they're short of… "You never say anything nice to me" points at words of affirmation; "we don't do anything together any more" points at quality time. The second clue is even more reliable: look at what they give you. People give spontaneously in their own language. Someone who makes you a coffee without being asked speaks acts of service, even if they have never once said so out loud.
section8.sub2Title: Which love language is the most common? And the rarest?
section8.sub2Text: Across the tens of thousands of questionnaires Chapman went through, two patterns keep coming back: quality time and words of affirmation come out on top, and receiving gifts trails at the bottom almost everywhere. Which says nothing about you, by the way. Being the only person you know who runs on gifts doesn't make your need any less serious. It just makes it less often understood.
section8.sub3Title: Can two languages come out tied?
section8.sub3Text: Yes, and it happens more often than people think. It means both genuinely reach you, not that the test got it wrong. When it does, use one very simple question: if you had to give up one of the two for good, which one would you miss more after a month? That one is your dominant language.
section8.sub4Title: Does your love language change over time?
section8.sub4Text: It does shift. Not overnight, but the big life stages move it. A first child usually pushes acts of service right up: when you no longer have an hour to yourself, someone emptying the dishwasher becomes a declaration. Living apart pushes words of affirmation up instead, because words are more or less all that fits down a phone line. Retaking the test every two or three years is not a silly idea.
section8.outro: One last piece of advice, and it's the one that changes the most: take the test separately, then compare the two charts. On your own it tells you something about yourself. Together it becomes an instruction manual.

jsonLd.quizDescription: Discover your love language among the 5 identified by Gary Chapman: Words of Affirmation, Acts of Service, Receiving Gifts, Quality Time, and Physical Touch.
jsonLd.faq1A: The 5 Love Languages are a theory developed by Gary Chapman that identifies five main ways of expressing and receiving love: Words of Affirmation, Acts of Service, Receiving Gifts, Quality Time, and Physical Touch. Each person has a dominant language that determines what makes them feel truly loved.
jsonLd.faq2Q: Can you have more than one love language?
jsonLd.faq2A: Yes, most people have a dominant language and a secondary one. It's completely normal to be responsive to several languages, even though one usually stands out. Your profile can also evolve over time and through life experiences.
jsonLd.faq3Q: What if my partner and I have different love languages?
jsonLd.faq3A: This is very common and perfectly normal. The key is learning to 'speak' the other person's language, even if it doesn't come naturally. Communicate openly about your respective needs and make small daily efforts to express your love in the language your partner understands best.
jsonLd.faq4Q: Can love languages change over time?
jsonLd.faq4A: Yes, love languages can shift over the years, particularly with major life changes (parenthood, moving, career shifts) and emotional growth. That's why it's a good idea to retake this test from time to time, to keep your mutual understanding up to date.

definition.texte: The 5 love languages are the five ways we express and receive affection: words of affirmation, acts of service, receiving gifts, quality time and physical touch. Everyone has a dominant one, and two partners rarely share the same, which explains a lot of misunderstandings.

lignes: A genuine compliment, a thank you, a note left on the table
A chore taken care of without being asked
A chosen token that proves you were on their mind
Forgotten dates, gifts grabbed at the last minute
Time together with no screens and real attention
Cancelled plans, a phone in the middle of dinner
A hand on the back, a hug, everyday closeness
Long stretches without contact, affection saved for the bedroom
tableau.note: No language is better than another: what matters is speaking your partner's rather than your own.
